narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 68.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but the school treated it as a strong reason not to admit you.

The most important factor was your third-year class standing. Being in the first decile—compared with accepted students who averaged around the sixth decile—pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor was your first-year class standing: again, first decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, and again in the failure direction. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor. At 38, it was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, so it nudged the prediction toward passing, but it was not strong enough to offset the class-standing concerns. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was above the accepted average of 3.23, but it was not among the top three influences.

To move forward, ask admissions whether you can request individual review and submit an explanation for your low class standing, including any upward trend or circumstances. Strengthen your record with additional rigorous coursework or legal-related experience, and speak with a pre-law advisor before reapplying. If you retake the LSAT, do so only after practice tests show a meaningful gain.
